title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Particle Beam Therapy versus Photon Radiotherapy for Skull Base Chordoma: TRP-Chordoma 2024
article_subtype: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression
condition_or_topic: Skull base chordoma treated with particle beam therapy (PT) or photon radiotherapy (RT)
clinical_background: Chordoma is rare, with an incidence of 0.18 to 0.84 per million people. It commonly arises in the sacrum or skull base and less often in the spine. NCCN guidelines recommend surgical resection as standard treatment and postoperative radiation when residual disease is suspected. Complete removal can be difficult at the skull base, while low radiosensitivity means that local control requires a dose of over 65 Gy and techniques that limit exposure to the brainstem and optic nerves. Particle beam therapy (PT) is frequently used because it concentrates the radiation dose. Although earlier meta-analyses favored PT over photon RT for chordoma across anatomical sites, none had compared them specifically for skull base chordoma. This site warrants separate study because onset tends to occur at a younger age, complete resection is harder to achieve, and postoperative RT is more often needed. Evidence combining skull base chordoma with chondrosarcoma may not apply directly because chondrosarcoma has greater radiosensitivity and better survival and local control.
objectives: Compare treatment outcomes with PT and photon RT for skull base chordoma using published evidence on outcomes and patient and treatment characteristics.
clinical_question: In patients with skull base chordoma, how does PT compare with photon RT or combined photon RT/proton beam therapy (PBT) for overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and late adverse events?
interpretation: For skull base chordoma, PT was associated with significantly better 5-year PFS than photon RT or combined photon RT/PBT, while treatment modality was not a significant predictor of 3-year or 5-year OS. The authors suggest that the PFS advantage may reflect the higher total doses and wider irradiation fields used with PT. They also report a tendency toward more brain necrosis after PT, which may offset some of its benefit.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier meta-analyses favored PT for chordoma without restricting the anatomical site, but the authors state that their analysis is the first to compare PT with photon RT specifically for skull base chordoma. They caution that findings from analyses combining chordoma with skull base chondrosarcoma may not apply directly to skull base chordoma. In a separate retrospective analysis by the authors, brain necrosis occurred in 13%, and higher total dose was identified as a risk factor. Previously published economic analyses associated the higher PFS achieved with PT in chordoma with favorable cost-effectiveness; the authors consider PT cost-effective for skull base chordoma despite its higher treatment cost.
clinical_implications: The observed improvement in 5-year PFS supports PT as an effective option for controlling skull base chordoma, although its higher tendency toward brain necrosis must be considered.

The authors suggest that greater total dose and broader target coverage may contribute to PT's PFS advantage, but these features may also increase normal-brain exposure and the risk of brain necrosis.

For curved or U-shaped targets, IMRT or combined photon RT and PBT may be useful. The authors note that spot-scanning IMPT can address planning limitations of passive PT without compromising tumor dose, although evidence for IMPT remains limited.
practice_implications: Plan PT carefully to minimize adverse effects, particularly brain necrosis.
Consider IMRT or combined photon RT and PBT when the target volume is curved or U-shaped, as the authors describe these approaches as potentially useful.
limitations: Skull base chordoma is rare, and the number of cases treated with photon RT was small.
Nearly all included studies were retrospective, limiting the quality of the analysis; the rarity of the disease also makes prospective studies difficult.
Many reports lacked information on dose fractionation, CTV settings and GTR rates, preventing a thorough assessment.
Missing data on GTR and tumor volume prevented their inclusion in the meta-regression, which was adjusted primarily for age and gender.
Too few studies of carbon ion therapy were available for a subgroup analysis by particle type.
strengths: The authors identify this as the first meta-analysis directly comparing PT and photon RT for skull base chordoma.
The authors state that meta-analysis allowed them to examine treatment outcomes despite the disease's rarity and the historical reliance on retrospective studies.
open_questions: Whether the reported PFS advantage and tendency toward brain necrosis will be confirmed in further studies.
How differences in surgical quality, including resection rates, affect treatment outcomes.
Whether proton and carbon ion therapy differ in biological effects and treatment outcomes.
Whether wider availability of IMPT will permit further dose increases and improve treatment outcomes.
future_directions: Publish and analyze further treatment studies to validate the findings.
Include surgical quality and resection rates in future analyses.
Assess outcomes by particle type when enough carbon ion therapy studies become available.
Evaluate IMPT further as clinical evidence becomes more widely available.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of published studies comparing particle beam therapy (PT) with photon radiotherapy (RT) for skull base chordoma. The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance and was not registered. Of the included studies, all but one were retrospective; one was prospective.

population.description: Patients with skull base chordoma treated with PT, photon RT, or combined photon RT/proton beam therapy (PBT). The initial screening also considered clinical studies of skull base chondrosarcoma.
inclusion_criteria: English-language articles published from 1990 to 2022 and identified through a PubMed search.
Clinical studies concerning chordoma or chondrosarcoma at the skull base.
Reports providing overall survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS).
Studies with ten or more cases per treatment modality.
Studies in which one treatment modality accounted for at least 80% of cases.
exclusion_criteria: When publications from the same institution covered overlapping periods, earlier reports were excluded in favor of the most recent study.

secondary: Late adverse events, including brain necrosis.

statistical_methods: Two reviewers independently screened retrieved articles. The investigators extracted case counts, survival outcomes, late adverse events, age, gender, gross total resection (GTR) rates, tumor volume, total irradiation dose, and treatment modality. They estimated 3- or 5-year OS and PFS from figures when these values were absent from the text. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted by modality for 3- and 5-year OS and PFS, with forest plots; I-square statistics assessed heterogeneity. Missing accuracy values were imputed using case counts, the risk set size at each year, and the mean dropout rate. Random-effects meta-regression compared modalities for each outcome, primarily adjusting for age and gender; GTR and tumor volume were excluded from that analysis because data were frequently missing. Analyses used R version 4.3.2 and its meta package.

document_sections.heading: Simple Summary
document_sections.content: Skull base chordoma is rare and difficult to treat because complete surgical removal is challenging and the tumor responds poorly to radiation. This comparison found better progression-free survival with particle beam therapy (PT) than with photon radiotherapy (RT), alongside a greater risk of brain necrosis. The findings suggest that PT offers better disease control, while treatment planning must address its potential adverse effects.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: The study compared PT with photon RT for skull base chordoma. The authors systematically reviewed reports published from 1990 to 2022 and extracted overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), late adverse events, age, gender, gross total resection (GTR) rates, tumor volume, total irradiation dose, and treatment modality. They used random-effects meta-regression with modality as an explanatory variable. Across 30 selected articles, 3-year OS was 90.8% (95% CI: 87.4–93.3%) with PT versus 89.5% (95% CI: 83.0–93.6%) with photon RT or combined photon RT/proton beam therapy (PBT), p = 0.6543. The corresponding 5-year OS figures were 80.0% (95% CI: 75.7–83.6%) versus 89.5% (95% CI: 83.0–93.6%), p = 0.6787. At 5 years, PFS was 67.8% (95% CI: 56.5–76.7%) with PT versus 40.2% (95% CI: 31.6–48.7%) with photon RT or photon RT/PBT, p = 0.0004. In the random-effects model, modality was not a significant factor for 3-year OS (p = 0.42) or 5-year OS (p = 0.11), but it was significant for 5-year PFS (p < 0.0001). Brain necrosis rates were 8–50% after PT and 0–4% after photon RT or photon RT/PBT. The authors conclude that PT yields higher PFS but tends to produce more brain necrosis; further published studies and analyses are needed to validate these findings.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Chordoma is rare, with an incidence of 0.18 to 0.84 per million people. It occurs most often in the sacrum and skull base, followed by the spine. NCCN guidelines recommend surgical resection as standard treatment and postoperative radiation when residual disease is suspected. Complete removal is difficult at common disease sites, and resistance to RT and chemotherapy complicates local control. Prognosis is significantly better after complete rather than incomplete resection. Postoperative RT is useful for skull base chordoma, but low radiosensitivity requires a dose of over 65 Gy for local control. Advanced irradiation techniques are therefore needed to deliver a high tumor dose while protecting structures such as the brainstem and optic nerves. PT is commonly used because it concentrates dose. Earlier meta-analyses reported an advantage for PT over photon RT in chordoma generally, but none had compared the modalities specifically for skull base chordoma. Relative to sacral or spinal chordoma, skull base disease has a younger age of onset, is harder to remove completely because of nearby anatomy, and more often requires postoperative RT. Although skull base chordoma is often treated similarly to skull base chondrosarcoma, chondrosarcoma is more radiosensitive and has clearly better survival and local control. The authors state that findings from meta-analyses combining these diseases may not apply directly to skull base chordoma. They therefore examined reported treatment outcomes and background characteristics to compare PT with photon RT specifically in skull base chordoma.

document_sections.heading: 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Selection Criteria for Meta-Analysis
document_sections.content: The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) principles and recommendations and was not registered. The authors searched PubMed for English-language articles published from 1990 to 2022 using “(chordoma OR chondrosarcoma) AND (radiotherapy OR proton OR carbon) AND (skull OR head)”. Two reviewers independently screened the retrieved papers. They first identified clinical studies of skull base chordoma or chondrosarcoma, then selected articles reporting OS or PFS. Eligible studies had ten or more cases per treatment modality, and a single modality had to account for at least 80% of cases. When publications from one institution covered overlapping periods, only the most recent was retained. Extracted information comprised case numbers, 3- or 5-year OS, 3- or 5-year PFS, late adverse events, age, gender, GTR rates, tumor volume, total irradiation dose, and modality, classified as PT versus photon RT or combined photon RT/PBT. When the article text did not specify 3- or 5-year OS or PFS, the authors estimated the rates from figures.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: For each modality, the authors performed random-effects meta-analyses of 3- and 5-year OS and PFS and produced forest plots. When accuracy data were missing, they imputed values using case numbers, the risk set size for each year, and the mean dropout rate. They assessed heterogeneity with I-square statistics and compared modalities through random-effects meta-regression using modality as an explanatory variable. Analyses used R version 4.3.2 and its meta package.

document_sections.heading: 3. Results
document_sections.content: The selection diagram describes how studies entered the review. Ultimately, 30 articles met the inclusion criteria: 17 focused on PT, 10 on photon RT, and 3 on combined photon RT and PBT. All but one study were retrospective; the exception was prospective. The selected-study table reports treatment modality, case numbers, patient and tumor characteristics, irradiation dose, survival, PFS, and brain necrosis for individual reports. The forest plots display OS by modality at 3 and 5 years and PFS by modality at the available time points. Pooled 3-year OS was 90.8% (95% CI: 87.4–93.3%) for PT versus 89.5% (95% CI: 83.0–93.6%) for photon RT or combined photon RT/PBT, p = 0.6543. Pooled 5-year OS was 80.0% (95% CI: 75.7–83.6%) versus 89.5% (95% CI: 83.0–93.6%), respectively, p = 0.6787. For PT, 3-year PFS was 71.7% (95% CI: 63.1–78.6%); insufficient data prevented calculation of the corresponding photon RT rate. At 5 years, PFS was 67.8% (95% CI: 56.5–76.7%) for PT versus 40.2% (95% CI: 31.6–48.7%) for photon RT or photon RT/PBT, p = 0.0004. Meta-regression was adjusted primarily for age and gender because extensive missing data prevented inclusion of potential variables such as GTR and tumor volume. Neither age nor gender was significant for any indicator. Modality was not significant for 3-year OS (p = 0.42) or 5-year OS (p = 0.11), whereas it was significant for 5-year PFS (p < 0.0001). The meta-regression table provides the predictive-factor analyses for OS and PFS. Brain necrosis, assessed as a late adverse event, occurred at rates of 8–50% in PT cases and 0–4% after photon RT.

document_sections.heading: 4. Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors describe this as the first meta-analysis directly comparing PT and photon RT for skull base chordoma. They argue that skull base disease warrants separate evaluation because it begins at a younger age and complete resection is less frequent than at other chordoma sites. PT has physical and biological properties useful at this location, but the disease’s rarity has hindered randomized comparisons. Their analysis found a significant 5-year PFS benefit with PT; PT outcomes were 90.8% for 3-year OS, 80.0% for 5-year OS, 71.7% for 3-year PFS, and 67.8% for 5-year PFS. The authors consider meta-analysis a way to examine the disease despite its rarity and the predominance of retrospective reports. They suggest that differences in total dose and irradiation field may explain PT’s better PFS. Median total doses in the analyzed reports ranged from 65–78.4 Gy relative biological effectiveness (RBE) for PT and 14.8–81 Gy (RBE) for photon RT or photon RT/PBT. Fraction doses varied, but total doses tended to be higher with PT. Reports using Gamma Knife or linear accelerator-based stereotactic radiosurgery and stereotactic radiotherapy (SRS/SRT) defined dose at tumor margins and delivered a higher dose centrally. In contrast, cited PT planning approaches commonly incorporated the pre-surgical tumor extent and a clinical target volume (CTV) margin of 5–10 mm around gross tumor volume (GTV). The authors propose that higher total dose and wider fields may account for the 5-year PFS difference. Cited reports also found the high PFS achieved with PT for chordoma favorable in cost-effectiveness terms. Although PT generally costs more than photon RT, the authors suggest that fewer reoperations and other procedures could offset costs. They note that some reports did not find substantial PT cost-effectiveness for head and neck cancer when outcomes were similar, whereas they consider it cost-effective for skull base chordoma. Greater brain necrosis after PT may partly offset its efficacy. The Bragg peak theoretically permits PT to concentrate a high tumor dose while limiting exposure of adjacent normal tissue. The authors’ separate retrospective analysis reported brain necrosis in 13% and identified high total dose as a risk factor. Exposure of normal brain to over 60 Gy is also a known risk factor, and a wider PT CTV may contribute. For a curved or U-shaped CTV, intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) may be effective, and combined photon RT and PBT may be useful. In particular, passive PT alone for a U-shaped target may leave underdosed areas when sparing the brain, potentially reducing local efficacy. The authors state that spot scanning with intensity-modulated particle beam therapy (IMPT) can overcome this limitation; cited work describes favorable skull base chordoma plans without compromising tumor dose. Although evidence for IMPT remains limited, the authors state that it provides better dose distributions to many organs than IMRT or passive PT. They anticipate that wider access to IMPT may permit further dose escalation and improved outcomes. Limitations include the rarity of skull base chordoma, the small number of photon RT cases, the difficulty of conducting prospective studies, and the retrospective design of nearly all included papers, which restricts analysis quality. Many reports lacked dose-fractionation, CTV-setting, and GTR-rate information, preventing a thorough analysis. Surgical details matter substantially to outcomes within integrated chordoma treatment; the authors anticipate future analyses of surgical quality, including resection rates, and note that outcomes improved with higher complete-resection rates in their earlier reports. A subgroup analysis comparing the biological effects of proton and carbon ion therapy could not be performed because too few carbon ion studies were available. Additional published outcomes may enable more detailed analyses.

document_sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
document_sections.content: For skull base chordoma, the authors conclude that particle beam therapy produces higher PFS than photon RT but also tends to cause brain necrosis more often. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings.

tables.title: Meta-regression estimates for factors associated with survival and progression-free survival
tables.summary: In the random-effects meta-regression, treatment modality was a significant factor for 5-year PFS, but not for 3-year OS or 5-year OS. Neither age nor male ratio was a significant factor for the assessed outcomes.

main_conclusion: For skull base chordoma, particle beam therapy was associated with higher progression-free survival than photon radiotherapy, alongside a tendency toward more brain necrosis. The authors state that further studies are needed to confirm these findings.
narrative_summary:
This systematic review and meta-analysis compared particle beam therapy (PT) with photon radiotherapy (RT), including studies of combined photon RT and proton beam therapy, for skull base chordoma. The authors selected 30 articles published from 1990 to 2022; 17 focused on PT, 10 on photon RT and 3 on combined treatment. All but one study were retrospective. They pooled survival outcomes using random-effects models and examined treatment modality through meta-regression adjusted primarily for age and gender.

At 5 years, progression-free survival was 67.8% (95% CI: 56.5–76.7%) with PT versus 40.2% (95% CI: 31.6–48.7%) with photon RT or combined treatment (p = 0.0004). Treatment modality remained a significant factor for 5-year progression-free survival in meta-regression (p < 0.0001), but not for 3-year overall survival (p = 0.42) or 5-year overall survival (p = 0.11). The reported brain necrosis rates were 8–50% after PT and 0–4% after photon RT. The authors suggest that higher total doses and broader treatment fields may contribute to the progression-free survival difference, while greater high-dose exposure of normal brain may contribute to necrosis. Interpretation is limited by the rarity of the disease, few photon RT cases, predominantly retrospective evidence and missing treatment and surgical details. The authors call for further studies to validate the efficacy and safety findings.
